facts.statement: The fossil remains of Astrophocaudia were discovered in the Paluxy Formation.
facts.quote: Its remains were discovered in the Paluxy Formation.

facts.statement: The specimens SMU 61732 and SMU 203/73655 were discovered and excavated by Robert Slaughter in the 1960s.
facts.quote: the specimens SMU 61732 and SMU 203/73655, which had been discovered and excavated from the Paluxy Formation of Texas by the paleontologist Robert Slaughter in the 1960s.

facts.statement: The species name slaughteri honors Robert Slaughter, who originally discovered the fossils.
facts.quote: The species epithet "slaughteri" is in honor of Robert Slaughter, the original discoverer of the remains.

facts.statement: The genus name means "non-twisting tail" because of the closely connected hyposphene-hypantrum articulation in the tail vertebrae.
facts.quote: The genus name as a whole therefore means "non-twisting tail", in reference to the closely-connected hyposphene-hypantrum articulation of the caudal vertebrae.

facts.statement: The genus name can also mean "star tail" because the tail vertebrae look like a three-pointed star when viewed from behind.
facts.quote: This second meaning is in reference to the shape of the caudal vertebrae when viewed from behind, which have the appearance of a three-pointed star.

facts.statement: Astrophocaudia is unique among sauropods due to the planar orientation of its tail vertebrae joints and specific laminae in front of the neural arches.
facts.quote: Astrophocaudia is able to be distinguished from all other sauropods by the following autapomorphies: a planar orientation of the hyposphene-hypantrum articulations relative to the zygapophyses and the presence of a lamina in front of the neural arches which contacts a second lamina between, and in front of, the zygapophyses.

facts.statement: Some researchers estimated the animal was about 10.9 meters long and weighed 2.85 tonnes.
facts.quote: Rubén Molina-Pérez and Asier Larramendi estimated the full size of this species at 10.9 m long and weighing 2.85 t.

facts.statement: Other researchers estimated the animal could have been up to 18.3 meters long and weighed 20 tonnes.
facts.quote: Evan Johnson-Ransom estimated a larger size of this species at 18.3 m long and weighing 20 t, making it comparable in size to Astrodon.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis places Astrophocaudia at the base of the Somphospondyli group, outside of Titanosauria.
facts.quote: He found that Astrophocaudia belonged in a polytomy at the base of Somphospondyli outside of Titanosauria.

facts.statement: This sauropod lived during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous in Texas, United States.
facts.quote: Astrophocaudia is an extinct genus of somphospondylan sauropod known from the later part of the Early Cretaceous (Albian stage) of Texas, United States.

facts.statement: It lived approximately 112 million years ago during the Early Cretaceous in what is now North America.
facts.quote: que vivió a principios del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 112 millones de años, en el Albiense, en lo que hoy es Norteamérica.

rejected.statement: Michael D. D'Emic, a doctoral student at the University of Michigan, re-examined the remains and described the new genus in 2012.
rejected.quote: The remains were re-examined by the doctoral student Michael D. D'Emic, who was studying at the University of Michigan at the time.

rejected.statement: The holotype consists of one tooth and a partial skeleton containing 24 tail vertebrae, 20 rib fragments, and other bones.
rejected.quote: The holotype of Astrophocaudia consists of a single tooth (SMU 203/73655) and a partial postcranial skeleton (SMU 61732).

rejected.statement: The fossil record indicates the animal lived between 113.2 and 110.1 million years ago.
rejected.quote: Time range: Albian to Albian (113.2 to 110.1 million years ago)
